extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate or beginning graduate students in dynamical systems / applied mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Study and exercise problems for discrete dynamical systems: orbit diagrams, bifurcations, Poincaré/return maps, homoclinic phenomena, the horseshoe map and symbolic dynamics. Includes worked constructions, theorems, and many exercises to verify behavior and prove chaotic dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find and classify periodic points
rubrics_metrics.description: Find all periodic points for a given map and classify them as attracting, repelling, or neither.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute periodic points by solving f^n(x)=x for relevant n; use linearization (derivative of f^n at the periodic point) to classify stability: |(f^n)'(x)|<1 attracting, >1 repelling, =1 neutral. Exercises explicitly ask this for many sample maps (e.g., Q(x)=x−x^2, C(x)=x^3−1, sin, exp, arctan, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and analyze bifurcations in parameterized families
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss the bifurcations that occur in one-parameter families of maps at indicated parameter values (e.g., S_λ(x)=λ sin x at λ=1, C_μ(x)=x^3+μx at μ=−1, E_λ(x)=λe^x at λ=1/e, A_λ(x)=λ arctan x at λ=±1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study how fixed points/cycles are created, destroyed, or change stability as parameter varies. Use linearization at fixed points, symmetry/exploiting oddness (hint given for C_μ), and check derivative/transversality conditions. The exercises instruct to 'discuss the bifurcations' and point to using the behavior of f and its derivatives at critical parameter values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saddle-node bifurcation theorem (conditions and conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Precise conditions under which a saddle-node bifurcation occurs for a smoothly parameterized family f_λ: existence of a fixed point at λ0, a unit multiplier, nondegeneracy, and a transversality condition imply the birth/annihilation of fixed points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up G(x,λ)=f_λ(x)−x and apply the Implicit Function Theorem at (x0,λ0). The textbook lists the standard hypothesis (fixed point at λ0, f'_(λ0)(x0)=1, and appropriate nondegeneracy/transversality conditions) and concludes there exists a smooth curve μ(x) with μ(x0)=λ0 giving parameter values where f_μ(x)(x)=x; µ'(x0)=0 and µ''(x0)≠0. Use this to prove typical local picture of fold/saddle-node.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify period-doubling (flip) bifurcation by explicit computation
rubrics_metrics.description: To verify a period-doubling bifurcation (e.g., for f_c(x)=x^2+c at c=−3/4 and c=−5/4), compute explicit period-2 orbits and analyze their stability across parameter ranges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute the period-2 points algebraically (solve f^2(x)=x but exclude fixed points), then evaluate the derivative of f^2 at those points to determine attracting/repelling for parameter intervals (exercise asks to show attracting for −5/4<c<−3/4). Use graphs of iterates (f^2, f^4) to detect subsequent period-doubling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce a continuous flow near a homoclinic orbit to a Poincaré (return) map
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct transit maps ψ1 and ψ2 between cross-sections (e.g., cylinder C and disk D) and compose them to obtain a Poincaré map Ψ=ψ2∘ψ1 on the cross-section; analyze this discrete map to deduce periodic orbits of the flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow solution curves from a cylinder C+ to a disk D+ (ψ1, using transit time τ from z(t)=z0 e^{2t}), then from D+ back to C (ψ2, assumed given). The composition Ψ defines the return map; fixed points of Ψ correspond to periodic solutions of the original flow. The section works out explicit formulas for ψ1, ψ2 and Ψ in polar/θ,z coordinates and uses them to find fixed points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of infinitely many periodic/ fixed points near a homoclinic orbit
rubrics_metrics.description: A homoclinic solution to a saddle-type equilibrium can produce infinitely many periodic orbits: the return map has infinitely many fixed points accumulating near the homoclinic tangency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the constructed Poincaré map Ψ the combination of terms like log(z0) and trigonometric factors causes the left-hand side of the fixed point equation to oscillate infinitely often as z0→0, guaranteeing infinitely many intersections and thus infinitely many fixed points. The text demonstrates this by squaring/adding the Ψ fixed-point equations and analyzing oscillation as z0→0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horseshoe map: geometric construction and dynamical consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition and prescription for the Smale horseshoe: contract horizontally by factor δ<1/2, expand vertically by 1/δ, bend back to form a horseshoe; preimage of S consists of two horizontal rectangles H0,H1 mapped to vertical components V0,V1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of linearity on the rectangles, iterated preimages produce 2^n thin horizontal strips (height ~δ^{n+1}) and images produce vertical Cantor-like sets. The invariant set Λ consisting of points whose entire forward/backward orbit stays in S is a Cantor set (product of Cantor sets), has symbolic coding, and supports chaotic dynamics. Use the detailed rectangle/strip geometry to reason about stable/unstable manifolds and intersections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic dynamics / itinerary conjugacy to the shift
rubrics_metrics.description: Associate to each point X in the invariant set Λ a (bi-infinite) itinerary (... s_{-2}s_{-1} · s_0 s_1 s_2 ...) with s_j∈{0,1}, and show the itinerary map S conjugates F|_Λ to the two-sided shift σ on {0,1}^Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define sj = k iff F^j(X) ∈ H_k. Impose a metric on sequences (weights 2^{-|i|}) so proximity corresponds to agreement on a long central block. Then S(F(X))=σ(S(X)), and S is a homeomorphism; consequently properties of the shift (2^n period-n points, dense orbit, topological mixing/chaos) transfer to F|_Λ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define forward-only, backward-only and full invariant Cantor sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct (Λ)^+ = ∩_{n≥0} F^{-n}(H0∪H1) (points whose forward orbit remains in S), (Λ)^- = ∩_{n≥1} F^{n}(H0∪H1) (points with backward orbit defined in S), and Λ = (Λ)^+ ∩ (Λ)^- (points with full orbit in S).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use preimage and image constructions: F^{-n}(Hi) yields 2^n strips of height δ^{n+1}, etc. The intersection over all n yields a Cantor set of horizontal (for Λ^+) or vertical (for Λ^-) line segments; their intersection Λ is a Cantor product set invariant under F.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stable and unstable sets; forward/backward asymptotic
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions: Z is forward asymptotic to X if |F^n(Z)-F^n(X)|→0 as n→∞ (and similarly backward asymptotic as n→−∞). Stable set W^s(X) = {Z | |F^n(Z)-F^n(X)| → 0 as n→∞}; unstable set W^u(X) defined analogously using backward iterates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the horseshoe picture, horizontal line segments through a point lie in its stable set; vertical segments lie in its unstable set. Preimages/images of these line segments generate many other pieces of W^s, W^u (e.g., F^{-k}(stable segment) yields 2^k intervals). Use symbolic description: sequences agreeing to the right of some index belong to W^s at the shift level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting periodic points via symbolic coding
rubrics_metrics.description: On the shift space (and hence on Λ) there are exactly 2^n periodic points of period n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A period-n sequence is any length-n block repeated bi-infinitely; there are 2^n such blocks. This yields exponential growth of periodic orbits and supplies dense periodic points in Λ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method: prove chaos by conjugacy to shift or by Cantor-set construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove a map is chaotic (in the sense used here) by demonstrating a conjugacy (or semi-conjugacy) to a shift map on symbolic sequences, or by constructing invariant Cantor sets with dense periodic orbits and sensitive dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The horseshoe and Lorenz-return-type maps are analyzed by exhibiting horseshoe-like geometry and coding or by showing a semi-conjugacy from the map onto the shift; exercises ask to show conjugacy, show density of periodic orbits, and deduce chaos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfolding/homoclinic bifurcations produce infinitely many bifurcations
rubrics_metrics.description: A one-parameter family F_λ of maps whose image moves from lying below a rectangle to crossing it (creating a horseshoe at λ=1) undergoes infinitely many bifurcations as λ varies from 0 to 1: no periodic points at λ=0, infinitely many at λ=1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand how the rising image creates intersections with preimages at many parameter values; the process 'unfolds' infinitely many horseshoe-like pieces and births of periodic orbits. The textbook remarks that the planar case is far more complex than the logistic one-dimensional family and is a subject of contemporary research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double scroll attractor: construction and properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Define A = closure ∪_{n≥0} Φ^n(C) and then A = ∪_{t∈R} φ_t(A) \ {(0,0,0)}; A is closed, invariant, contains ω-limits of points in C, and has volume zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute determinant of derivative of the Poincaré map (here det DΦ = 1/8) to see areas shrink, hence the attractor has zero two-dimensional area in the section and zero volume in R^3. The set behaves like an attractor except possibly transitivity; it is called the double-scroll attractor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of binary expansions for the doubling map
rubrics_metrics.description: For the doubling map D on [0,1), represent x in binary as a0 a1 a2 ... and observe D shifts the binary expansion left. This explains which points are periodic and why finite-precision computer arithmetic causes orbits to eventually land at 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give explicit formula for binary of D(x): D shifts digits, discarding the leading digit. Finite binary precision forces truncation/rounding, so after finitely many iterations the representation becomes all zeros and the computer orbit becomes fixed at 0. Exercises ask to list periodic points and those that end up at 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify linear maps f_k(x)=k x by parameter regimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Show there are four open parameter sets for which orbit behavior of f_k is qualitatively similar; describe exceptional cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze cases by |k| relative to 1, sign of k, and special values k=±1, k=0; deduce contraction to 0 (|k|<1), expansion to infinity or divergence (|k|>1), and neutral/degenerate behavior at exceptional k. Exercise prompts explicit description of these four open sets and exceptional cases.
